title: What Is It Like? Describing, comparing and measuring materials

summary.text: This unit is about properties. A property is a word for what a material is like, such as hard, bendy, shiny or waterproof. You find out a property by looking, touching, listening and testing. Better still, you can measure it, so you can say which material is harder, stronger or thirstier, and by how much. Every material has many properties at once, and the job decides which ones matter. Properties come from the tiny atoms inside a material and how they are joined. Scientists can measure most properties very well. But they still cannot predict them all in advance, and they still argue about what glass really is.
summary.art: A split picture: on the left a child's hands testing a steel spoon, a cotton cloth and a glass bangle on a table; on the right a magnified view of the same three materials, showing a crowd of atoms in each, arranged differently.

intro.hook: Try this. Pick up a steel spoon in one hand and a wooden spoon in the other. They have been in the same room all day. Which one feels colder? Now guess what a thermometer would say.
intro.text: About three hundred years ago, in Bengal, weavers made a cloth so fine that people called it woven air. Stories say a whole sari could be pulled through a finger ring. But the thread for this cloth had a strange habit. In the cool morning it held strong. At noon it kept snapping. Nobody could say why. Was the cotton bad? Were the spinners tired? Or did the thread itself change with the hour? To solve it, you need the idea this unit is about: the properties of a material, and how to measure them.
intro.art: A river village at dawn, mist on the water. A woman and a girl sit on a mat, spinning cotton into thread so thin it can barely be seen against the light. A long piece of fine cloth lies on the grass beside them, the grass showing through it.

outcomes: I can say what a property is, and name at least ten properties of materials.
I can tell an object from the material it is made of, and say which properties belong to the material.
I can compare two materials in one property, and put several in order from most to least.
I can measure a property with a simple test, and write the result as a number with a unit.
I can explain that no property is good or bad on its own, because the job decides which one matters.
I can give examples of properties that change with thickness, wetness or heat.
I can say where properties come from: atoms and how they are joined. And I can name something scientists still cannot predict.

terms.meaning: A material is what a thing is made of. Steel, wood, glass, cotton and clay are materials.
terms.example: A spoon is an object. Steel is the material it is made of.
terms.art: A steel spoon with an arrow pointing to the word 'object' and a block of steel with an arrow pointing to the word 'material'.

terms.meaning: An object is one thing with a shape and a use, like a spoon, a tumbler or a bangle.
terms.example: A steel tumbler and a steel spoon are two objects. They are made of the same material.
terms.art: A steel tumbler and a steel spoon side by side, joined by a glowing label 'steel'.

terms.meaning: A property is a word that tells what a material is like. You find it out by looking, touching, listening or testing.
terms.example: Hard, shiny and heavy are all properties of steel.
terms.art: A steel spoon with four small labels: hard, shiny, heavy, rings when tapped.

terms.meaning: Hard means hard to scratch or dent.
terms.example: A steel nail is hard. A bar of soap is not.
terms.art: A nail scratching a bar of soap and leaving a groove, while the soap cannot scratch the nail.

terms.meaning: Soft means easy to scratch, dent or squash.
terms.example: Chalk is soft. Your fingernail can scratch it.
terms.art: A fingernail leaving a white line on a stick of chalk.

terms.meaning: Rigid means stiff. A rigid thing keeps its shape and does not bend easily.
terms.example: A stone step and a thick wooden plank are rigid.
terms.art: A hand pushing on a thick wooden plank that does not move.

terms.meaning: Flexible means it bends easily and does not break.
terms.example: A cotton cloth, a rubber band and a plastic ruler are flexible.
terms.art: A plastic ruler bent into a curve in two hands.

terms.meaning: Elastic means it gets longer or bends when you pull it, and springs back when you let go.
terms.example: A rubber band and a hair tie are elastic.
terms.art: A rubber band stretched between two fingers, and the same band relaxed beside it.

terms.meaning: A strong material can hold a big pull or push without breaking. A weak material breaks with a small one.
terms.example: A steel rope is strong. A thin sewing thread is weak.
terms.art: A steel rope holding a heavy bucket and a thin thread snapping under a small weight.

terms.meaning: Brittle means it snaps or shatters instead of bending.
terms.example: A glass bangle, a dry biscuit and a stick of chalk are brittle.
terms.art: A glass bangle dropped on a stone floor and breaking into pieces.

terms.meaning: Texture is how the surface of a material feels. It can be rough, smooth, bumpy, silky or fluffy.
terms.example: Sandpaper is rough. A polished marble floor is smooth.
terms.art: A hand on sandpaper next to a hand on smooth marble.

terms.meaning: A shiny surface bounces light back like a mirror. A dull surface does not.
terms.example: A steel tumbler is shiny. A clay brick is dull.
terms.art: A steel tumbler with a bright reflection beside a dull red brick.

terms.meaning: You can see clearly through a transparent material.
terms.example: Window glass and clean water are transparent.
terms.art: A child looking through a clear window at a tree outside.

terms.meaning: Light comes through a translucent material, but you cannot see clearly through it.
terms.example: Butter paper and a frosted bathroom window are translucent.
terms.art: A torch shining through butter paper and making a soft blurry glow.

terms.meaning: No light comes through an opaque material.
terms.example: A steel plate and a wooden door are opaque.
terms.art: A torch shining on a steel plate and making a dark shadow behind it.

terms.meaning: A waterproof material does not let water in or through.
terms.example: A plastic raincoat and a rubber boot are waterproof.
terms.art: Raindrops rolling off a plastic raincoat.

terms.meaning: An absorbent material soaks up liquid into its tiny gaps.
terms.example: A cotton towel, a sponge and a paper towel are absorbent.
terms.art: A paper towel soaking up a puddle of spilled water.

terms.meaning: A conductor of heat lets heat flow through it quickly.
terms.example: A steel spoon in hot tea gets hot at the handle very soon.
terms.art: A steel spoon in a cup of hot tea with glowing arrows moving up the handle.

terms.meaning: An insulator of heat lets heat flow through it slowly.
terms.example: Wood, plastic and wool are insulators. That is why a pan has a wooden handle.
terms.art: A kadhai on a flame with a wooden handle that stays cool.

terms.meaning: A thing floats if it stays on top of water. It sinks if it goes to the bottom.
terms.example: A cork floats. A steel nail sinks.
terms.art: A cork floating in a bowl of water beside a nail resting on the bottom.

terms.meaning: To measure is to find out how much, using a number and a unit.
terms.example: The card bent down by 4 centimetres. The number is 4. The unit is centimetres.
terms.art: A ruler held beside a bent cardboard strip, showing the number 4.

terms.meaning: A scale puts things in order, from least to most, so we can compare them.
terms.example: The Mohs scale puts minerals in order from 1, the softest, to 10, the hardest.
terms.art: A ladder with ten rungs, with a soft mineral at the bottom and a diamond at the top.

terms.meaning: A fibre is a thin strand, like a hair. Cotton, wool, paper and wood are all made of fibres.
terms.example: A cotton thread is many tiny fibres twisted together.
terms.art: A magnified cotton thread showing many short fibres twisted together.

terms.meaning: Atoms are the tiny building blocks of every material. They are far too small to see.
terms.example: A single grain of sand has far more atoms in it than there are people on Earth.
terms.art: A cotton thread, then a zoom into a fibre, then a zoom into a pattern of tiny balls joined together.

explanations.definition: A property is a word that tells what a material is like.
explanations.description: You can find out a property in four ways. You can look, touch, listen or test. Some you see at once, like shiny or see-through. Others need a test, like strong or waterproof. A property belongs to the material, not to one object. A steel spoon and a steel tumbler have different shapes. But both are hard and shiny, because both are steel.
examples: Look: a steel spoon is shiny and a brick is dull.
Touch: sandpaper is rough and marble is smooth.
Listen: a steel spoon rings when tapped and a wooden spoon makes a dull knock.
Test: drip water on a plastic bag and on a cotton cloth, and see which one soaks it up.
explanations.art: Four panels: an eye looking at a spoon, a hand on sandpaper, an ear next to a tapped spoon, and water dripping on a cloth.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: what a property is and how we find one out.

explanations.concept: One material, many properties, and the job decides
explanations.definition: Every material has many properties at the same time. The job decides which of them matter.
explanations.description: Steel is hard, strong, shiny, heavy and stiff. It also carries heat well and feels cold. For a bridge, strength matters most. For a kadhai, carrying heat matters most. No property is good or bad by itself. Paper is weak, and that is useful for tissue paper, because a gift is easy to open. Cotton is thirsty, which is perfect for a towel but wrong for a raincoat.
examples: A window needs glass to be see-through. It does not matter that glass breaks easily, as long as it is not hit.
A towel needs cotton to be absorbent. A raincoat needs plastic to be waterproof.
A cricket bat needs wood that is strong but a little springy.
explanations.art: A steel object in the middle with six small labels around it: hard, strong, shiny, heavy, stiff, carries heat. Two of the labels are circled for a bridge and a different two for a kadhai.
explanations.context: This card is about why the same material can be right for one job and wrong for another.

explanations.concept: Hard and soft: the scratch ladder
explanations.definition: A material is hard if it is hard to scratch. If material A scratches material B, then A is harder than B.
explanations.description: You can put any materials in order of hardness with one simple test. Try to scratch each with the others. In 1812 a German mineral expert called Friedrich Mohs did this with ten minerals. He put talc at 1, the softest, and diamond at 10, the hardest. Now anyone can place a new mineral on the ladder. A fingernail is about 2 and a half. A steel nail is somewhere around 4 to 5. Ruby and sapphire are 9. Diamond is far harder than 9, not just one step more. The numbers only give the order.
examples: Your fingernail scratches soap and chalk, so it is harder than both.
A diamond scratches everything, so it sits at the top of the ladder.
Ruby and sapphire are the same mineral, called corundum. Only the colour is different.
explanations.art: A ladder with rungs labelled soap, chalk, fingernail, steel nail, glass, quartz, ruby and diamond, a small arrow showing which one scratches which.
explanations.context: This card explains what 'hard' means and how to compare hardness with a scratch test.

explanations.definition: A flexible material bends easily. An elastic material springs back to its shape after bending or stretching.
explanations.description: Bendy and springy are not the same. A rubber band is both. It stretches, then springs back. Aluminium foil is flexible but not elastic. It bends easily and stays bent. A thick steel ruler is stiff, but if you bend it a little, it springs back. Bend it too far and it stays bent. Bend it much too far and it snaps. Try bending a paper clip back and forth. It gets warm, and then it breaks. Your bending put energy into the metal as heat.
examples: Clay and dough are flexible but not elastic. They keep any new shape.
A bamboo pole bends in the wind and springs back, so it can be used for scaffolding.
A glass bangle does not bend at all. It breaks. That is called brittle.
explanations.art: Four strips: a rubber band that springs back, aluminium foil that stays bent, a steel ruler that springs back, and a glass bangle that snaps.
explanations.context: This card is about the differences between rigid, flexible, elastic and brittle.

explanations.concept: Strong is not the same as hard
explanations.definition: A strong material holds a big pull or push without breaking. Hard means hard to scratch. They are different properties.
explanations.description: Glass is hard. A nail cannot scratch it easily. But glass is not strong against a knock. It shatters, because it is brittle. A cotton rope is soft, but it can hold a bullock cart. Strength also depends on size. A thick thread holds more than a thin thread of the same cotton. So when we compare strength, we cut the strips to the same width and length. Steel is both hard and strong, and that is why it is used so much.
examples: A glass tumbler is hard but breaks when dropped.
A jute rope is soft but strong.
A chalk stick is soft and weak.
explanations.art: Three pictures: a glass tumbler shattered on a floor, a soft jute rope pulling a heavy sack, and a steel chain holding an anchor.
explanations.context: This card clears up a common mix-up between strong and hard.

explanations.concept: Light through things: transparent, translucent, opaque
explanations.definition: A transparent material lets light through so you can see clearly. A translucent one lets light through but blurred. An opaque one lets no light through.
explanations.description: When light meets a material, three things can happen. It can go straight through. It can be scattered, which means it bounces off in all directions. Or it can be soaked up. Clear glass lets nearly all light go straight through. Butter paper scatters it, so you see a glow but no picture. A steel plate soaks up or bounces back all of it. Thickness matters too. One sheet of butter paper is translucent. A tall stack of sheets is opaque. Even clear sea water is dark by the time you go down about a thousand metres.
examples: A frosted bathroom window lets in light but hides you.
Morning mist is translucent when thin and almost opaque when thick.
A stone jaali screen lets in light and air but keeps a room private.
explanations.art: Three torches shining on clear glass, butter paper and a steel plate, with the spot of light on a wall behind each one: sharp, blurry and none.
explanations.context: This card explains the three light words and why thickness matters.

explanations.concept: Inside the material: why glass is clear and metal is shiny
explanations.definition: How a material treats light depends on how its electrons behave.
explanations.description: Electrons are tiny charged specks inside every atom. In glass, the electrons are held tightly. Light of the colours we can see does not have the right energy to shake them. So the light passes through, and glass is clear. In a metal, some electrons are not tied to any one atom. They roam like a crowd in a market. When light arrives, the crowd shakes and throws the light straight back. That is why metals look shiny. The same roaming electrons carry heat, which is why metals feel cold, and they let atoms slide past each other, which is why metals can be hammered into shape. This is a simple picture. The full story needs quantum physics.
examples: A polished steel tumbler acts like a poor mirror.
A brass puja bell rings for a long time and can be hammered into a bowl.
Thin gold leaf, used on sweets, is so thin that light can shine through it.
explanations.art: Two magnified panels: in glass, light passing through rows of tightly held electrons; in metal, light bouncing off a crowd of free electrons moving between atoms.
explanations.context: This card zooms inside materials to show why they look and feel the way they do.

explanations.definition: An absorbent material soaks liquid into its tiny gaps. A waterproof material keeps liquid out.
explanations.description: Cotton, paper and sponge are full of tiny gaps between fibres. Water is pulled into the gaps and climbs up through them, even against gravity. This climbing is called wicking. A plastic bag has no gaps, so water stays on top. Some leaves are waterproof in a clever way. A colocasia leaf, called arbi in many kitchens, is covered in tiny wax bumps. Water cannot spread out on it, so it rolls into a ball and runs off. Scientists copied this idea to make paint and cloth that stay dry.
examples: A diya wick draws oil up by wicking.
A clay matka is a little absorbent. Water seeps to the outside and cools the pot as it dries.
A lotus leaf and a colocasia leaf keep dust off because rolling drops carry it away.
explanations.art: Left: a paper towel dipped in water with water climbing up it. Right: a round drop of water beading on a colocasia leaf.
explanations.context: This card explains why some things soak up water and some do not.

explanations.concept: Water's skin and the girl who measured it
explanations.definition: Surface tension is the pull between the particles on the surface of water, which makes the surface behave like a stretchy skin.
explanations.description: Look at a drop on a leaf. Its surface holds together like a thin skin. That is why a needle can float on still water, and why a pond insect can walk on it. About 135 years ago, a young woman called Agnes Pockels, who lived in Germany, measured this skin in her kitchen. Women in Germany were not allowed into university. She used a tin tray, a balance and buttons. She found that a drop of oil or soap on the water changes its skin. In 1891 she wrote to Lord Rayleigh, a famous British physicist, and he helped her get her work printed in the journal Nature. Later, a famous scientist built on her kind of tray and won a Nobel Prize. She did not.
examples: A water strider insect stands on a pond without sinking.
A drop of dish soap makes the skin weaker, so a floating pepper pinch runs away from it.
Soap lets water soak into cloth, because it weakens the skin.
explanations.art: A girl in an old-fashioned kitchen bending over a tin tray of water, balancing buttons on a tiny scale, with a magnified drop of water beside her showing a stretchy skin.
explanations.context: This card is about why water forms drops and bubbles, and about the woman who first measured it carefully.

explanations.definition: A conductor of heat lets heat flow through quickly. An insulator lets it flow slowly.
explanations.description: Heat always flows from the warmer thing to the cooler thing. In a room, a steel spoon and a wooden spoon are the same temperature. But the steel spoon feels colder. Your hand is warmer than the spoon. Steel carries the heat away from your hand very fast. Wood carries it away slowly. So your skin tells you about how fast heat leaves, and not about the real temperature. Metals are good conductors. Wood, plastic, wool, cloth and air are good insulators. Diamond conducts heat even better than copper. On the Moon, a probe on India's Chandrayaan-3 lander found the top of the soil was about 70 degrees Celsius. Just eight centimetres down, it was about 10 degrees below zero. Moon soil is a very good insulator.
examples: A kadhai has a wooden or plastic handle to stop heat reaching your hand.
Woollen clothes keep you warm because they trap air, and air is a poor conductor.
A steel plate left in the freezer feels much colder than a plastic one.
explanations.art: Two spoons in a mug of hot water: the steel one with glowing arrows running up the handle and a hand pulling back, the wooden one with no arrows.
explanations.context: This card explains why metal feels cold and wood feels warm, even in the same room.

explanations.definition: A thing floats on water if it is less packed with stuff than the same amount of water. We say it is less dense.
explanations.description: A big ship floats, but a small stone sinks. So weight is not the answer. What matters is how much stuff is packed into a space. A stone is packed tight. A ship is mostly air inside, so on average it is less packed than water. That is why one lump of aluminium foil sinks, but the same foil folded into a boat floats. The material is the same. The object is different. Ice floats too, which is unusual. Most solids sink in their own liquid, but ice floats on water. Lakes freeze from the top, and fish survive underneath.
examples: A coconut floats and a stone of the same size sinks.
A steel ship floats, because its hollow shape holds air.
A lump of plasticine sinks, but a plasticine boat floats.
explanations.art: A foil ball sinking in a bowl of water and a foil boat floating beside it.
explanations.context: This card explains why some things float, and why it is not just about being heavy.

explanations.concept: From words to numbers: measuring a property
explanations.definition: To measure a property is to give it a number and a unit, so that anyone can repeat the test and get the same answer.
explanations.description: Words like 'harder' or 'more bendy' are a start. But numbers let us say how much, and let other people check. More than four thousand years ago, traders in the cities of the Indus Valley used neat cubes of stone as weights, in a regular system. A buyer and a seller in two different towns could trust them. A good measure uses the same size of sample, the same method, and the same unit each time. We repeat it three times, because one try can be a fluke. If the three numbers are close, we trust them. We call that reliable.
examples: How far a card droops, in centimetres.
How many marbles a paper strip can hold before it tears.
How many layers of paper it takes to block a torch.
explanations.art: A trader in an Indus Valley market weighing goods with small stone cubes on a balance, next to a child weighing marbles on a modern one.
explanations.context: This card explains why scientists use numbers and units for properties, and how to trust a measurement.

explanations.concept: Same atoms, different properties: diamond and pencil lead
explanations.definition: A material's properties come from which atoms it has and how those atoms are joined together.
explanations.description: A diamond and the black lead of a pencil are both made only of carbon atoms. Yet diamond is the hardest natural material and graphite, the pencil lead, is so soft that it rubs off on paper. In a diamond, every atom is joined strongly to four neighbours, in all directions, like a locked climbing frame. In graphite, the atoms lie in flat sheets. Within a sheet the joins are strong, but the sheets slide over each other like cards in a pack. In 1913, a father and son, William Henry Bragg and William Lawrence Bragg, used X-rays to find the pattern inside a diamond. Later, Kathleen Lonsdale, who became one of the first two women elected to the Royal Society in 1945, used X-rays to study how atoms are arranged in many crystals, including diamond.
examples: Press your pencil lightly and the sheets slide off onto paper. That is how a pencil writes.
A diamond can cut glass because it is the hardest natural material.
A single sheet of graphite one atom thick is called graphene. It was first peeled off with sticky tape in 2004.
explanations.art: Two magnified pictures of carbon atoms: a 3D locked framework labelled diamond and flat layered sheets sliding over each other labelled graphite.
explanations.context: This card shows how the same atoms can make very different materials, and how scientists found out.

explanations.definition: A rubber band is stretchy because it is made of very long, tangled chains of atoms that uncoil when pulled and tangle up again when let go.
explanations.description: Rubber comes from the milky sap of the rubber tree. The sap is made of very long chains of atoms, like a bowl of cooked noodles. When you pull the band, the noodles straighten out. When you let go, they tangle up again, because a tangle is the more likely arrangement. Here is a strange fact. Stretch a thick rubber band fast, then touch it to your lip. It feels warm. Let it go quickly and it feels cool. Stretching and tangling change how the atoms jiggle, and that changes the heat.
examples: Rubber tyres, chappals and balloons are all stretchy.
Cotton and wool are made of fibres that can be twisted into thread.
Spider silk is a protein chain that can stretch and is very strong.
explanations.art: A rubber band stretched across the page, with a magnified view above showing long tangled noodle-like chains straightening out as the band is pulled.
explanations.context: This card zooms inside a rubber band to show why it springs back.

explanations.concept: Properties change: thickness, wetness and heat
explanations.definition: A property is not always the same. It can change when the thickness, the wetness or the temperature changes.
explanations.description: One sheet of butter paper is translucent. A tall stack is opaque. A dry cotton thread is weaker than the same thread when it is damp. Warm wax is soft and cold wax is hard. A blacksmith heats iron until it glows, and then it is soft enough to hammer. This is why a good scientist always writes down how the test was done. 'This thread held 11 seeds' means little. 'This thread, as long as my forearm, in the damp morning air, held 11 seeds' means a lot.
examples: Wet paper is much weaker than dry paper.
Chocolate is hard in the fridge and soft in your hand.
Glass is hard and brittle at room temperature, but a glassblower shapes it when it glows.
explanations.art: Three pairs of pictures: one sheet and a tall stack of butter paper on a torch, dry thread and damp thread holding different weights, cold wax and warm wax.
explanations.context: This card explains why the same material can behave differently in different conditions.

explanations.description: Scientists agree on how to measure strength. They do not agree on the winner, because 'strongest' can mean many things. Strongest for its weight? Strongest for its thickness? Strongest that anyone has actually touched? Different answers give different winners. Three of the best claims are very different from each other.
examples: Steel holds up bridges and buildings.
A spider's dragline silk is thinner than a hair and tough enough to stop a flying insect.
Graphene is one atom thick.

perspectives.explanation: For building things, the best material is the one that does the job cheaply and safely. So steel and concrete still win.

perspectives.who: Biologists and material scientists studying spider silk
perspectives.explanation: Weight for weight, spider silk is among the toughest fibres known. A spider makes it at room temperature from a fly's meal. People still cannot copy it exactly.
They poked a single sheet of graphene with a tiny diamond tip. They found it was the strongest material ever measured, for its thickness. Sheets this perfect are very hard to make large.
Deep inside a dead star there may be a material called nuclear pasta. Their simulations say it could be billions of times stronger than steel. Nobody has ever touched it, and nobody can.

explanations.art: Four small pictures in a row: a steel bridge, a spider hanging on a thread, a sheet of graphene as a chicken-wire pattern, and a neutron star with a swirl of pasta-like shapes in a cut-away.
explanations.context: This card asks which material is the strongest of all. Scientists give different answers.

explanations.concept: Materials that grow: bone, wood and shell
explanations.definition: Living things make their own materials, with properties that engineers admire.
explanations.description: Your bones are a material your body builds and repairs. Bone is made of a hard mineral, which resists squashing, and a bendy protein called collagen, which stops it snapping. Together they are tough and light. The outside of your teeth, called enamel, is the hardest material your body makes. Wood is made of long thin cells with strong walls, like bundles of straws. The inside of a sea shell, called mother-of-pearl, is made of tiny chalky tiles stuck together with a stretchy glue. It is much harder to crack than the plain chalk it is made from. Nature builds from the bottom up, atom by atom.
examples: Bengal craftspeople have carved bangles from conch shell for centuries.
A bamboo stem is hollow and strong because of its fibres.
A hen's eggshell is thin but hard to crush if you press the ends.
explanations.art: A cut-away of a bone showing a lattice of hard mineral with flexible fibres, a shell with brick-like layers, and a bamboo stem cut across showing bundled fibres.
explanations.context: This card is about living things as makers of materials.

agreed.text: Every material has properties that we can find out by looking, touching, listening and testing.
agreed.evidence: Craftspeople have done this for thousands of years. Laboratories today get the same answers with machines. Anyone can repeat a scratch test or a bend test and get the same order.

agreed.text: A property can change with thickness, wetness and temperature, so a test must say how it was done.
agreed.evidence: One sheet of butter paper lets light through and a tall stack does not. Cotton thread is stronger when damp than when dry. Textile scientists have measured this for a hundred years.

agreed.text: Hard, strong, stiff and tough are different properties, and one does not tell you the others.
agreed.evidence: Glass is hard but breaks when dropped. A rope is soft but strong. Engineers measure each one with its own test.

agreed.text: Properties come from the atoms a material has and how they are joined.
agreed.evidence: In 1913 the Braggs used X-rays to see the pattern of atoms in a diamond. Diamond and pencil lead are both carbon, and the pattern is the only difference.

agreed.text: Measuring with numbers and units lets different people compare and trust each other's results.
agreed.evidence: The Indus Valley traders used standard stone weights more than four thousand years ago. Every science laboratory today does the same with standard units.

challenging.claim: Metal is colder than wood, even in the same room.
challenging.who: Almost everybody, because it feels true every time we touch a metal gate on a winter morning.
challenging.for: A steel spoon feels much colder than a wooden one when you pick it up.
challenging.against: A thermometer reads the same for both. Metal feels colder only because it pulls heat out of your hand faster. Your skin is a poor thermometer. It tells you how fast heat is leaving, not what the temperature is.
challenging.context: This card looks at a very common belief about metal, and what a test shows.

challenging.who: A common idea, and very easy to believe because steel is both.
challenging.for: The hardest materials we know, like diamond, are used for cutting and drilling. Hard things feel solid and strong.
challenging.against: Glass is hard but shatters when dropped. A diamond can crack if it is hit on the right side. A cotton rope is soft but can hold a bullock cart. Hard means hard to scratch. Strong means hard to break by pulling or pushing.
challenging.context: This card looks at a mix-up between two properties, hard and strong.

challenging.claim: Heavy things sink and light things float.
challenging.who: Most young children, and many grown-ups when they are not thinking.
challenging.for: A stone sinks and a feather floats. A coin sinks and a leaf floats.
challenging.against: A huge steel ship weighs thousands of tonnes and floats. A tiny pebble sinks. A big log floats and a small nail sinks. What matters is how much stuff is packed into the space, not how heavy a thing is.
challenging.context: This card looks at a famous guess about floating and sinking, and why it fails.

challenging.claim: A material always has the same property, wherever and whenever you test it.
challenging.who: A natural way of thinking, which we all use when we say 'steel is strong'.
challenging.for: Steel is nearly always strong. Glass nearly always breaks. These words are useful.
challenging.against: Properties change with thickness, wetness and heat. A dry cotton thread is weaker than a damp one. Hot iron is soft. A thin sheet of any material is more bendy than a thick one. So a good scientist says how the test was done.
challenging.context: This card looks at the idea that a property is a fixed fact about a material.

challenging.claim: A property belongs to a thing all by itself, whether or not anything is touching it.
challenging.who: Most of us, when we say 'this stone is hard'. Some thinkers, like the Buddhist teacher Nagarjuna (about the 2nd century CE), looked at it differently.
challenging.for: A stone seems hard even in a dark cupboard where nobody is testing it. Its atoms are joined the same way whether anyone scratches it or not.
challenging.against: 'Hard' means 'harder than something else'. 'Cold' means 'takes heat from a warm hand'. A thread is strong in damp air and weak in dry air. A property shows up in a meeting between two things. Nagarjuna taught that nothing exists all alone, and everything depends on other things. Most scientists would add that the stone has a real structure that decides what happens in every meeting.
challenging.context: This card asks a deep question: is a property inside a thing, or does it only show up when two things meet?

challenging.who: A guess many people make, because wet paper and wet cardboard fall apart.
challenging.for: Wet paper tears. Wet cardboard goes soft. Wet mud is weak.
challenging.against: Wet cotton thread is stronger than dry. In the story of this unit, damp air saved the muslin spinners. Damp sand is harder to dig and carry than dry sand, and the Egyptians poured water on sand to pull heavy stone on sledges. Water can help or harm, depending on the material.
challenging.context: This card looks at the idea that water is always a problem for materials.

challenging.claim: A wonder material like graphene will soon replace the old ones.
challenging.who: Many news stories and some companies since 2004, when graphene was first made.
challenging.for: Graphene is very thin, very strong, bendy and nearly clear. It carries heat and electricity very well.
challenging.against: It is hard and costly to make big, perfect sheets. Steel, wood and glass are cheap, strong enough and easy to make. In twenty years graphene has found some uses, but most of the early promises have not come true yet. Scientists still debate how big its future will be.
challenging.context: This card looks at big promises about a new material and what has happened since.

big_questions.q: A diamond scratches glass. Glass scratches chalk. So is glass hard or soft?
big_questions.hint: Hard compared with what? Try placing glass on a ladder with chalk below it and diamond above it.

big_questions.q: A diamond and the black lead of a pencil are both pure carbon. How can the same atoms make one of the hardest things and one of the softest?
big_questions.hint: Think of the same bricks. You can build a strong wall, or just pile them in a heap. What changes?

big_questions.q: A steel spoon and a wooden spoon are the same temperature, but the steel spoon feels colder. What is your hand really feeling?
big_questions.hint: Your hand is warmer than the spoon. Which spoon takes the warmth away faster?

big_questions.q: Glass and wood are both made of atoms. Why can light go through glass but not through a wooden door?
big_questions.hint: Light has to get past the tiny electrons. In glass they are held tight. In wood, they and the fibres soak up and scatter the light.

big_questions.q: If nobody ever scratched a stone, would it still be hard?
big_questions.hint: A property is what would happen if you tested it. Is that the same as what is happening right now?

big_questions.q: Is a thread that snaps easily weak, or just wrong for some jobs? Could that be true of people too?
big_questions.hint: Paper is weak, and tissue paper is useful because it tears easily. Which job suits you well?

big_questions.q: Long ago, traders in different towns had different weights. Why is it fairer when everyone uses the same units?
big_questions.hint: Imagine a shopkeeper whose kilogram weighs less than yours. Who is helped, and who is cheated?

big_questions.q: Soft water cut the hard rock of the Grand Canyon. How can a soft thing beat a hard thing?
big_questions.hint: Water is soft, but it carries sand. It also has a very, very long time.

big_questions.q: Deep inside a dead star there may be a material stronger than any on Earth. Nobody can ever touch it. How can we know about it?
big_questions.hint: We can use rules we have tested on Earth, and a computer, to work out what must happen. How sure should we be?

big_questions.q: Your bones are a material that your body builds and mends. What other things around you are grown rather than made?
big_questions.hint: Wood, cotton, wool, silk, leather, bamboo, shell, pearl. Which ones do you wear or use?

big_questions.q: In the story, was the thread's strength in the thread, in the air, or in the two together? And what about your own strengths?
big_questions.hint: The same thread was strong at dawn and weak at noon. Do you act the same in every place and with every person? Which parts of you are really yours?

big_questions.q: Every diamond, pencil lead and soot is carbon. If everything is made of just a few kinds of atom, are all the many things really one thing in different patterns?
big_questions.hint: Think of the same letters making many words. Where does the word live, in the letters or in the pattern?

big_questions.q: In our story, a ten-year-old found out why the thread broke when the grown-ups blamed the cotton. Why do you think nobody asked her sooner?
big_questions.hint: Think about who gets listened to. Who can see things that others miss?

story.title: The Thread That Held at Dawn
story.note: Real: the muslin of Bengal and its names Abrawan, Shabnam and Baft Hawa. Real: the weavers worked near rivers and the best spinning was done in the damp of early morning and evening. Real: wet cotton is stronger than dry. Real: gunja seeds were used for centuries as small weights. Imagined: Shefali, her aunt Pishi, the village and the merchant's agent, and the counting test.
text: About three hundred years ago, a village stood on a wide brown river in Bengal, not far from a town called Sonargaon. The people there made a cloth so fine that merchants carried it across the sea. Its names were poems. One was Abrawan, flowing water. One was Shabnam, evening dew. One was Baft Hawa, woven air.

Shefali was ten. She lived with her aunt, her Pishi, in a house with walls of woven bamboo. Pishi was the best spinner in the village. She could pull a bundle of cotton into thread so thin that you only saw it when the light fell sideways. Shefali's jobs were small ones. She cleaned the cotton, she fetched water, and she kept quiet while her aunt worked.

One morning, a merchant's agent came walking up from the river. He wore a clean white cloth and carried a thin silver ring. 'The Nawab's household wants one piece,' he said. 'The finest ever made. When it is finished, I must be able to pull all of it through this ring, in one breath.' He set the ring down on the mat. 'Do this, and you will be paid in silver. Fail, and the order goes to the next village.' Everyone looked at Pishi.

Pishi began at once. In the first grey light, the thread came out like a hair of mist and held. Shefali watched it with her breath held too. But as the sun climbed, something went wrong. The thread began to snap. It snapped on the spindle. It snapped on the loom. Pishi tied it, spun again, and it snapped again. By noon, the mat was covered in little broken ends, like white hairs.

The village had opinions. 'The cotton is bad,' said the neighbour. 'Her hands are tired,' said another. 'The river is angry,' said a third. Pishi said nothing. But Shefali saw her hands shake, and she knew they were not tired hands. They were the same hands that had spun the dawn thread.

That night, Shefali could not sleep. She thought about it the way you pull at a knot. If the cotton was bad, it would have been bad at dawn. If the hands were tired, they would have been tired at dawn. Same cotton. Same hands. So something else had changed between the morning and the noon. What?

She did not know. But she knew one way to find out. Her father was a trader, and he had taught her to weigh small things with gunja seeds, the little red seeds with a black spot. Every seed weighs the same as the next one. Goldsmiths have used them for hundreds of years.

Before sunrise, she got up. She cut a piece of thread as long as her forearm. She tied a little shell to the bottom, and she hung the thread from a bamboo pole. Then she dropped gunja seeds into the shell, one at a time, and counted out loud. At seven seeds, the thread shivered. At ten, it was still there. At eleven, it snapped. She wrote the number in the dust. Then she did it with a second thread, and a third. Ten, eleven, eleven.

At noon, she did it all again, with threads from the same ball of cotton, each cut to the same forearm's length. The first one held six seeds. The second, seven. The third, five. The dawn threads held nearly twice as many.

Shefali ran to Pishi. 'Count with me,' she said. 'The thread is stronger at dawn.' Pishi had never counted a thread before. She watched the red seeds fall, one by one, and her face slowly changed. 'It is the air,' said Shefali. 'In the morning the air by the river is wet. At noon it is dry. Maybe the thread likes the water.' She dipped a noon thread in a bowl and tested it again. It held nine.

Pishi was quiet for a long time. Then she said, 'My teacher used to say that the thread loves the river. I thought she was speaking poetry.' She looked at the seeds in the dust. 'Perhaps she was speaking the truth in the only words she had.'

After that, the village changed its hours. They spun before sunrise, and again in the evening when the mist rose off the river. At noon, they rested. The weavers set their looms close to the water and kept little bowls beside them, to touch the thread with damp fingers. Pishi spun the finest thread of her life. And every evening, she let Shefali count the seeds on each new spool.

Weeks later, the cloth was finished. The agent held it up, and it was so fine that he could see his own hand through it, as if through mist. When it was spread on the grass, the grass showed through. He lifted a corner and drew all of it through the silver ring in one breath. The ring did not even touch it. He paid in silver, and the cloth went away down the river and across the sea.

Nobody wrote down Pishi's name, or Shefali's. The cloth got a name, and a price, and an owner far away. But in the village the hours stayed, and the mothers said to their daughters, 'Spin while the air is wet.' They did not say why, because by then nobody remembered who had counted.

That kind of muslin is no longer made. The last masters grew old, the special cotton nearly vanished, and the world changed. Today, weavers and scientists are trying to bring it back, and the first thing they have to learn is what Shefali learned. A thread has a strength. But the strength depends on the air it lives in.
story.epiphany: For the parent: a property is not a fixed fact. The strength of cotton thread changes with the dampness of the air. The grown-ups guessed, and blamed the cotton, the hands and the river. Shefali counted. She used the same length, the same seeds and the same method every time, so that the numbers could be compared. Only then could the real cause show up. The story also quietly asks who gets heard, and who gets named.
ask: In the story, the thread snapped at noon but not at dawn. What did Shefali think had changed?
How did Shefali make her test fair? Why did she cut every thread to the same length?
Why did she count seeds, and not just say 'this one is stronger'?
Everyone in the village had a guess. Why was a number better than a guess?
Is the thread's strength in the thread, in the air, or in both together? What do you think?
Nobody wrote down Shefali's name. Who does a small job at your home that makes everything else work?

games.title: Property Snap
games.players: 2 to 5 players, or one child playing against a grown-up
games.context: This is a matching card game about properties. Each property has three cards: its name, a test that shows it, and an example. You collect complete sets by asking other players for cards.

printables.title: 36 cards to cut out: 12 properties, with 3 cards each
items: TEST: Try to scratch it with your fingernail. You cannot.
TEST: Push on the middle. It hardly bends at all.
TEST: Bend it. It bends easily and does not break.
TEST: Stretch it, then let go. It springs back.
TEST: Bend it too far. It snaps into pieces.
TEST: Hang weights from it. It holds a lot before it tears.
TEST: Hold it in front of a torch. A clear, bright spot shows on the wall.
TEST: Hold it in front of a torch. A blurry glow shows on the wall.
TEST: Hold it in front of a torch. Only a shadow shows on the wall.
TEST: Drip water on it. The drop stays on top.
TEST: Drip water on it. The drop soaks in.
TEST: Look at it in the light. You can see a bright reflection.

printables.title: 6 challenge cards
items: Glass is hard but breaks when dropped. Which two properties is that?
A rubber band and a cotton cloth can both be bent. Which one is elastic, and how do you know?
A plastic bag and a paper towel both look thin. How do you test which is waterproof?
Butter paper is translucent. How could you make it opaque?
A rope is soft but strong. A chalk stick is hard to bend but weak. Explain.
Name a material that is both rigid and brittle, and one that is both rigid and not brittle.

rules: Shuffle the 36 cards. Deal 5 to each player. Put the rest face down in a pile.
A set is three cards for the same property: its WORD, its TEST and its EXAMPLE.
On your turn, ask one player for a card. You must name the property and the kind. For example, 'Do you have the TEST for brittle?'
If they have it, they give it to you and you ask again. If not, you draw a card and your turn ends.
When you have a complete set, lay it down. Read all three cards out loud. Take a score token.
If you get a challenge card, answer it. A good answer wins a bonus token. When all the sets are laid down, the player with the most tokens wins.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 36 cards. 2. Read the 12 property names together. 3. For each one, read its test and its example. 4. Shuffle and deal 5 cards each.
flow.say: A property is a word for what a material is like. There are twelve here. Each has a name, a test and an example. Let's read them all before we play.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Read the twelve property names. Read each test and each example. Then deal.
flow.context: This is the first step of Property Snap. It is a matching game where you collect a name, a test and an example for each property. Here you set up and read the cards.

flow.do: Play one practice turn together. Ask: which TEST goes with 'translucent'?
flow.say: Let's practise. Here is one card: 'Hold it in front of a torch. A blurry glow shows on the wall.' Which property does it test?
flow.kid: Read the test card. Which property does it show? Tap your answer.

check.q: Hold it in front of a torch. A blurry glow shows on the wall. Which property is that?
check.why: A blurry glow means some light comes through, but it is scattered. That is translucent. A clear bright spot would mean transparent. Only a shadow would mean opaque. Picking 'transparent' usually means thinking anything that lets light through is the same.

flow.do: Play the game. When you lay down a set, read all three cards aloud and say whether you agree that the test and the example fit.
flow.say: Remember to say the property and the kind of card you are asking for. If you disagree with a match, say why.
flow.kid: Take turns. Ask for a card by name and kind. Lay down each complete set and read it aloud.
flow.parent: Good habit: when a set is laid down, ask the table 'Would that test really show that property?' This is the heart of the game, not the winning.

flow.do: Take a challenge card. Read it aloud and let the table discuss the answer before anyone reveals it.
flow.say: Here is a tricky card. Talk about it together first. Then someone can say the answer.
flow.kid: A challenge card! Talk about it together. Then answer.

ask.q: Which pair of properties did you find hardest to tell apart?
good: Hard and strong.
Elastic and flexible.
Waterproof and the opposite, absorbent.

flow.parent: Key answers. Hard means hard to scratch, and brittle means it snaps, so glass is hard and brittle. A rubber band is elastic because it springs back, and cloth is only flexible because it stays bent. Test waterproof by dripping water on it. Butter paper turns opaque in a tall stack.

flow.do: Count the tokens to find the winner. Talk about which tests you remembered most easily.
flow.say: Which tests were easy to remember? Which were hard? Which two properties look alike?
flow.kid: Count your tokens. Which tests were easy to remember? Which were tricky?
flow.think: If you could only do three tests on a mystery material, which three would you choose?

setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards. Read the name, test and example for each property.

setup.art: A child holding five cards and asking another player across the table, with a speech bubble that says 'TEST for brittle?'
setup.caption: 2. Ask another player for a card. Say the property and the kind of card.

games.title: Property Trumps
games.context: This is a card game. Each card is a material with scores from 0 to 5 for five properties. You pick a property and the highest score wins the round.

printables.title: 16 material cards to cut out, with rough scores for fun
items: Steel: hard 5, bendy 1, see-through 0, thirsty 0, strong 5
Aluminium foil: hard 2, bendy 5, see-through 0, thirsty 0, strong 1
Copper: hard 3, bendy 3, see-through 0, thirsty 0, strong 4
Glass: hard 5, bendy 0, see-through 5, thirsty 0, strong 2
Clear plastic: hard 2, bendy 3, see-through 4, thirsty 0, strong 3
Wood: hard 3, bendy 1, see-through 0, thirsty 2, strong 4
Bamboo: hard 3, bendy 3, see-through 0, thirsty 1, strong 4
Cotton cloth: hard 1, bendy 5, see-through 1, thirsty 5, strong 3
Wool: hard 1, bendy 5, see-through 0, thirsty 4, strong 2
Newspaper: hard 1, bendy 4, see-through 1, thirsty 4, strong 1
Paper towel: hard 1, bendy 5, see-through 1, thirsty 5, strong 1

printables.title: A score sheet with a column for each player and a row for each round
items: Why that material scores high or low

rules: Deal all the cards. Each player holds their pile face up, so they see only the top card.
The first player picks one property from their top card and reads out its score. They must say why the material scores high or low. For example, 'Steel, hard 5, because a nail cannot scratch it.'
Everyone else reads out the same property from their top card. The highest score wins all the top cards.
If there is a tie, put the cards in the middle. The next winner takes them too.
The scores on these cards are rough guesses, for fun. You will make a better set from real measurements in the project.
The player with the most cards after 15 minutes wins.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 16 cards. 2. Read the five properties together: hard, bendy, see-through, thirsty (soaks up water) and strong (holds a big pull). 3. Shuffle and deal.
flow.say: Each card gives a material five scores. Zero means none at all. Five means a lot. Thirsty means soaks up water. Strong means it holds a big pull without breaking.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Learn the five properties. Zero means none. Five means a lot. Then deal the cards.
flow.context: This is the first step of Property Trumps. It is a card game where you compare the scores of materials. Here you set up and learn the five properties.

flow.do: Play one practice round. Show the top cards. Ask: 'If I chose thirsty, who would win?'
flow.say: Let's practise with one round. Look at your top cards. If I pick 'thirsty', who wins?
flow.kid: Look at your top cards. If we pick 'thirsty', who wins? Tap your answer.

check.q: Cotton cloth is thirsty 5. Clear plastic is thirsty 0. In a round on 'thirsty', who wins?
options: Cotton cloth, because it soaks up the most water
Clear plastic, because it keeps water out
check.why: 'Thirsty' means soaks up water, so the higher number soaks up more. Cotton scores 5. Picking plastic usually means mixing up 'thirsty' with 'good at keeping water out'. That property is waterproof, the opposite.

flow.do: Play the game. Before each round, the chooser says why their material scores high or low. If anyone disagrees with a score, test it for real if you can.
flow.say: Remember to say why. Why is steel strong 5? Why is glass bendy 0? If you disagree with a score, say what you would change.
flow.kid: Take turns. Choose a property. Say why your material scores high or low.
flow.parent: Good reasons: steel is hard 5 because a nail cannot scratch it, glass is bendy 0 because it snaps, and cotton is thirsty 5 because it soaks up water. Diamond is the joker. It scores high for almost everything, because it is the hardest natural material and is clear.

flow.do: Look at the cards. Is there a material with a 5 for everything? Is there a material with a 0 for everything?
flow.say: Look through the cards. Is there a perfect material that wins every round?
flow.kid: Look at all the cards. Is there one that wins every round? Why not?

ask.q: Why can no material be the best at everything?
good: Some properties pull in opposite directions.
A very bendy thing cannot also be very stiff.
Each job needs different properties.

flow.think: Which two properties on these cards never seem to go together?
